title: Weighted Ballot Problem: Setup and Motivation
content: Introduces the weighted ballot problem: what happens when votes have non-unit rational weights? The classical ballot theorem (Bertrand 1887, André 1887) gives $(a-b)/(a+b)$ for unit-weight votes, relying on the combinatorial symmetry of $\pm 1$ sequences. This file demonstrates that the formula breaks for non-uniform weights, identifies why the fiber counting argument fails, and establishes the scaled ballot expression as a partial generalization. All structural facts are verified by `decide` and `norm_num` with 0 sorries and 0 axioms.
mathContext: The classical ballot theorem: if candidate $A$ gets $a$ votes and $B$ gets $b$ votes with $a > b$, the probability that $A$ leads throughout the count is $(a-b)/(a+b)$. The weighted version replaces unit votes with rational weights $w_1, \ldots, w_{a+b}$.

title: Weighted Ballot Sequences and Goodness
content: Defines the core abstractions: `WeightSeq` as a list of rationals (positive for A-votes, negative for B-votes), `partialSums` via `scanl` (running totals), and `isGoodWeighted` requiring all partial sums to be strictly positive (A leads throughout). The `Decidable` instance enables verification by `decide` and `native_decide`, which is critical for the counterexample verification.
mathContext: A weighted ballot sequence $(w_1, \ldots, w_n)$ is 'good' if $\sum_{i=1}^k w_i > 0$ for all $1 \le k \le n$. This is the weighted analogue of the classical condition that $A$'s running total is always positive.

title: Counterexample: Classical Formula Fails for Non-Uniform Weights
content: Exhibits a concrete counterexample defeating the classical formula. Configuration: $A$ has votes with weights $[2, 1]$ ($W_A = 3$) and $B$ has one vote with weight $[2]$ ($W_B = 2$). All $3! = 6$ orderings are enumerated, and each is verified good or not good by `decide`. Result: 2 good orderings out of 6, giving $P = 1/3$, while the classical formula predicts $(3-2)/(3+2) = 1/5$. The discrepancy $1/3 \ne 1/5$ is verified by `norm_num`.

title: Fiber Argument Failure: Why the Classical Proof Breaks
content: Formalizes the structural reason the classical proof fails: the 'fiber argument' from the parent OQ-02 file requires that each $\pm 1$ sign pattern has equally many good refinements. For non-uniform weights, this is false. The theorem `projection_ambiguity` shows $[2, -1]$ is good but $[1, -2]$ is not, despite having the same $[+, -]$ sign pattern. `fiber_argument_fails` packages this as an existential witness.
mathContext: The parent proof maps each multi-candidate ordering to a $\pm 1$ pattern and argues the fibers (refinements of a given pattern) have uniform goodness. For weighted sequences: $[2,-1]$ has partial sums $[2, 1]$ (good) while $[1,-2]$ has $[1, -1]$ (bad), yet both project to $[+, -]$. The fiber is not uniform $\Rightarrow$ the probability transfer fails.

title: 1-vs-1 Case: Exact Analysis with General Weights
content: Analyzes the simplest non-trivial case: one $A$-vote (weight $w_A$) vs one $B$-vote (weight $w_B$) with $w_A > w_B > 0$. Of the 2 orderings, exactly one is good (proved via `two_good_iff`), so the actual $P = 1/2$. The classical formula gives $(w_A - w_B)/(w_A + w_B) = 1/2$ iff $w_A = 3w_B$, providing another demonstration that the formula fails except in a measure-zero set of weight configurations.
mathContext: For 1-vs-1: $P = 1/2$ always (one ordering is good, the other bad). The formula $(w_A - w_B)/(w_A + w_B) = 1/2 \Leftrightarrow w_A - w_B = (w_A + w_B)/2 \Leftrightarrow w_A = 3w_B$. So the formula is correct only when $w_A/w_B = 3$.

title: Scaled Ballot Expression and Open Directions
content: Defines `scaledBallotFormula a b p q = (ap - bq)/(ap + bq)` and proves three properties: degeneration to the classical formula when $p = q = 1$, positivity when $ap > bq$, and the probability bound $\le 1$. Importantly, the docstring warns this is an expression with nice algebraic properties, NOT the actual ballot probability for the scaled case. An explicit counterexample ($a=2, b=1, p=2, q=1$) shows the expression gives $3/5$ while the actual probability is $2/3$. Concludes with open directions.
mathContext: The scaled expression $(ap - bq)/(ap + bq)$ degenerates to $(a-b)/(a+b)$ when $p = q = 1$. But for $a = 2, b = 1, p = 2, q = 1$: expression $= (4-1)/(4+1) = 3/5$, while the actual probability (from the classical theorem with $a = 2, b = 1$) is $(2-1)/(2+1) = 1/3$ — wait, that's the unweighted probability. The scaled case is genuinely different from both.
